#3157. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3156. NEURA plans a robot training gym in Spain with Aragón’s government

Companies will train robots on their own tasks there, and can license the skills they build to others.

Representatives of NEURA Robotics, the Government of Aragón and Costa Group sign the memorandum of understanding.

German robotics firm NEURA Robotics has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government of Aragón and agri-food group Costa Group to open a NEURA Gym in Aragón by mid-2027. The partners plan to invest in the double-digit millions of euros, with NEURA leading, and to add a zone for testing robots in real settings.

German robotics company NEURA Robotics plans to open a robot training centre in Aragón, Spain, by mid-2027, it said on Thursday. It has signed a memorandum of understanding with the regional government and Costa Group, an Aragonese meat and agri-food group.

The partners plan to invest in the “double-digit millions of euros”, with NEURA taking the lead. They did not give an exact figure.

The site will be one of NEURA’s Gyms, where companies train robots on real tasks before putting them to work. Firms will bring their own processes, test them on different robots and check how well they perform.

Through NEURA’s Neuraverse platform, companies can keep the robot skills they develop private or license them to others for a fee.

“A company that develops a valuable skill should benefit when others use it,” said David Reger, NEURA’s founder and chief executive.

Costa Group will supply real problems from its farms and factories. The first projects will aim to cut physically demanding and repetitive work, before moving into logistics, cars and manufacturing. The University of Zaragoza will add research and train staff.

The partners also plan a “Physical AI Model Zone”, where robots can be tested in real working settings. Its scope and locations are still to be agreed, and any testing in public areas will need permits.

NEURA raised up to $1.4B in June, partly to expand its Gyms. It has since bought two companies. In Spain, Barcelona’s THEKER raised €73M in June for factory robots that learn on the job.

#3155. Apple’s new ‘HomeView’ is exactly the home product I’ve been waiting for

Apple has launched several exciting new products in the last month, including iPhone Duo and the redesigned MacBook Pro. But my personal favorite new product is Apple’s HomeView. Here’s how I’ve been using it.

Two years ago when Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on Apple’s forthcoming HomeView, I was immediately ready to buy one.

After numerous delays, the HomeView is finally here. And despite several shortcomings I expect will be fixed with software updates, the HomeView overall is exactly what I’ve been wanting in a home product.

HomeView is essentially a HomePod, but with a screen. And that screen adds so much extra value.

When rumors said the HomeView would only have a 7-inch display, I was concerned it would be too small. It turns out, Apple knew what it was doing. The HomeView’s size is a feature, not a bug. Too much larger and it would stand out as a piece of tech. By staying small, the HomeView can be a cute, non-distracting addition to the home.

Here are some HomeView features I’ve been loving so far:

None of these is what I’d call a “killer feature,” but together they amount to a delightful experience. I already liked having a HomePod around, and HomeView builds on that foundation in so many ways.

Overall, HomeView is very much the product I was hoping for back in 2024. That said, there’s definitely room for improvement. Here’s what’s missing.

I love HomeView for what it is today, but I fully expect Apple to improve the product via software updates. Leaks already point to two major feature upgrades in the works that I hope ship soon.

Built-in apps for Apple Photos and Notes would be great to have, plus support for the recipes included in Apple News+. But my personal top request is for parental controls of some sort.

I completely agree, this is exactly the device I’ve been waiting for.

My only con… Siri AI is just slightly more than half-baked when it comes to voice prompts. One example, when we ask it for the weather forecast it gives us a one-line “It’s going to rain today.” That’s not a forecast. 🙃 So we’re forced to follow up with “more details please”. When we do… 🙂 … we get an actual forecast. Asking it for a recap of today’s headlines is hit or miss too. These are just two of a handful of examples where Siri AI is only about 60% of what Alexa+ is for conversational AI purposes.

With that one nod to the nut jobs out there claiming an old iPad suffices everyone on planet earth perfectly well, I’m still giddy about the fact that I can browse through my full library of music on Apple Music, Amazon Music, and iBroadcast and try new “suggested” albums/playlists without having to have my iPhone with me everywhere I go in the house. While I spent $299 mainly for an enhanced music experience, having it is priceless.

For a device that’s intended for the whole family, I’ve been surprised to find there are no current features to prevent young children from doing whatever they want with HomeView. I have a toddler who loves the HomeView so much that I had to move it out of his reach. I wish there was a way to lock the screen on command, or prevent switching apps or faces without authentication. Some sort of “toddler mode” would be greatly appreciated.

Siri AI has also had some bugs, but those are likely related to me running the iOS 27.3 beta.

Apple’s new HomeView is available now for $299.

What’s your take on the HomeView so far? Are you still mulling a purchase? Let us know in the comments.

#3153. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

#3151. Verizon is in talks to buy fibre operator Fidium for $6B, FT reports

The deal would add to Verizon's Frontier purchase as its home internet growth lags rivals.

Verizon is in talks to buy Fidium, a fibre broadband operator owned by Searchlight Capital and BCI, for about $6B including debt, the Financial Times reported. A deal could come within weeks, as Verizon tries to win more home internet customers after buying Frontier.

Verizon is in talks to buy US fibre broadband operator Fidium for about $6B including debt, the Financial Times reported on Friday, according to Bloomberg.

Fidium is owned by Searchlight Capital Partners and British Columbia Investment Management Corporation (BCI). A deal could come in the coming weeks, the FT said, though another bidder may emerge and the talks may not lead to a takeover.

Verizon declined to comment. Fidium did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.

The Illinois-based company sells fibre internet in more than 20 US states. It was called Consolidated Communications until last year, when it renamed itself after its fibre brand. Searchlight and BCI agreed to take it private in 2023 in a $3.1B deal including debt.

Verizon has been buying fibre networks to catch up with rivals in home internet. Earlier this year, it closed its $9.6B purchase of Frontier Communications.

Growth has still been slow. Verizon added 314,000 broadband customers in the third quarter, below analysts’ estimates, even as it signed up twice as many new phone customers as expected.

Chief executive Dan Schulman told investors that customers increasingly prefer fibre to 5G-powered home internet. Since taking over last year, Schulman has cut retail jobs and argued that SpaceX would need up to $500B to match Verizon’s mobile network.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

#3148. macOS 27.3 adds three new Mac features, here’s what’s coming

macOS 27.3 is launching next month alongside iOS 27.3 and more, and it includes a variety of new features for Mac users. Here are three macOS 27.3 features coming soon.

macOS already supports running Live Activities from your iPhone via iPhone Mirroring. But in macOS 27.3, Apple is adding native support for Live Activities from Mac apps.

The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the new Dynamic Island. But with macOS 27.3, the new feature expands to all Mac models and in a slightly different way.

Live Activities on Macs without a Dynamic Island will display in the menu bar. From there you can click to view full details, as seen above.

Safari introduces several upgrades across macOS 27.3, iOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3.

Vertical Tabs are one tentpole addition, providing a new option for how to view your tabs in Apple’s browser. When enabled, your tabs move from the top of the browser to the left side in a new column view.

Adaptive Dark Mode is another new feature. It automatically enables dark mode on many websites that don’t natively support it already. Finally, Siri AI gains support for new Safari actions, including the ability to interact with a full webpage using onscreen awareness, not just the parts that are currently visible.

Do you use Markdown, the popular John Gruber-created plain text syntax? If so, macOS 27.3 has a welcome addition: support for rendering Markdown in Quick Look.

Rather than needing to open Markdown files in apps to preview formatted text, macOS now lets you just use Quick Look and see all of your Markdown syntax rendered properly with links, headings, bold, italics, and more.

You can learn more about Markdown here on John Gruber’s site, Daring Fireball.

Which macOS 27.3 additions are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3147. OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers

Counterclaims filed in San Jose turn Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit into a two-way fight.

OpenAI has filed counterclaims against Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers not to work on OpenAI’s devices and using broad employment agreements to stop engineers joining OpenAI, Bloomberg reported. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging theft of hardware trade secrets.

OpenAI says Apple has pushed suppliers not to work on its devices, Bloomberg reported. It made the claims in a court filing in San Jose on Friday, hitting back at Apple’s trade-secrets lawsuit.

“Apple has responded to OpenAI’s anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI,” the company said in the filing.

According to OpenAI, Apple asks suppliers to name their OpenAI projects and the staff on them who once worked for Apple. It then tries to keep anyone who has worked on OpenAI products off Apple jobs. That makes suppliers wary of putting staff on OpenAI work.

One supplier moved its OpenAI work to the night shift so it would not overlap with Apple work, which raised OpenAI’s costs, the filing says. Others have moved meetings with OpenAI so Apple would not see them.

OpenAI also takes aim at the contracts Apple staff sign. It says they treat almost everything workers learn as secret and stop them hiring away Apple staff for a year. It repeats its claim that a former worker who returned to Apple took more than 100 files about an unreleased OpenAI device.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg. It has said before that it found no evidence for OpenAI’s claims.

Apple sued in July. It says OpenAI and its hardware chief Tang Tan used former Apple staff to get its secrets, and that OpenAI had a shared supplier copy an Apple metal-finishing method. In October, OpenAI agreed not to use the files Apple says were taken while the case goes on.

The fight hangs over OpenAI’s plans to sell devices designed with Jony Ive, starting with a doughnut-shaped speaker. The two once worked together to bring ChatGPT to Siri, a partnership that has since turned sour.

#3146. iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m currently using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer …

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

What I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

The size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

My preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen

While the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I said when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

It’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an issue at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI ).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

The aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the new Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

The Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The issue is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

The rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the issue, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

One of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller issue than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

I said in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

I’m where you are. I received mine on Tuesday. It’s too heavy. It’s too expensive, especially with a subpar camera. Touch ID is annoying. The larger screen is going to be rarely used in my day-to-day. Giving up the larger main screen for a screen I’ll rarely use for an extra $1000 seems kinda dumb.

But every so often I open an app or webpage on the larger screen and it’s pretty amazing.

I’ll probably return it. But my choice isn’t the duo or the 18 Pro. By doing away with the iPhone upgrade program and not releasing a pro phone with groundbreaking advancements Apple has removed my incentive to move to the 18. If I send the Duo back I’ll keep my 17 Pro, and see what the Air 2 offers. Much like I moved from the larger, heavier MBP to the smaller, lighter MBA when its power far surpassed what I need I may do the same with my phone if the next gen of the iPhone Air is compelling enough.

My head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

In previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

Weight is the most important consideration when buying a weighted blanket. It should weigh roughly 10% of your overall body weight, to ensure you can comfortably move underneath it.

And be aware that weighted blankets can trap heat. You might find this adds to the coziness but for hot sleepers, we recommend looking for a weighted blanket with cooling covers.

#3143. Three new iPhones will launch early next year, here’s what’s coming

Apple recently launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but three more new iPhone models will reportedly arrive in early 2027. Here’s what’s coming.

iPhone 18 was conspicuously absent from Apple’s annual September event this year. Instead, the company launched iPhone 18 Pro and kept iPhone 17 around as the base model.

But the iPhone 18 is still coming, expected to launch in early 2027—likely February or March.

The basic design of the iPhone 18 is expected to stay unchanged as Apple prioritizes internal upgrades. Rumored new features include a more powerful A20 chip with at least a slight RAM bump, plus increased battery life.

We’re not expecting iPhone 18 Pro’s camera upgrades, smaller Dynamic Island, or vapor chamber to come to the base model. One question mark is the C2 cellular modem. iPhone 17 uses a Qualcomm modem, and it’s unclear whether that will be the case with iPhone 18 as well.

Apple also has a lower-cost iPhone 18e model reportedly in the works. It’s expected to launch around the same time as iPhone 18.

Reporting indicates the iPhone 18 and 18e might be more similar than prior corresponding models. Improvements coming to the 18e include:

ProMotion is expected to be missing from the new model, which will still have a 60Hz display. And while big rear camera upgrades are unlikely, a recent CAD leak suggests iPhone 18e might get a larger camera bump.

The iPhone Air 2 will reportedly aim to address two of the top wishes users had for the first-gen model. Those two upgrades are:

By adding a second rear camera, iPhone Air 2 will at least offer camera parity with the base iPhone—something the original Air couldn’t with its single camera.

Battery life gains could ease concerns about the iPhone Air 2 running a full day on a charge. And hopefully the Air 2 will benefit from positive word-of-mouth about the first model.

Another tentpole addition is the A20 Pro chip, which might include one less GPU core than iPhone 18 Pro but otherwise be very similar.

Following the introduction of these three iPhone models in early 2027, Apple is expected to launch new Pro and Duo models in fall 2027.

Are you interested in buying any of these upcoming iPhone models? Let us know in the comments.

#3141. Top Wall Street analysts find these 3 stocks attractive as long-term investments

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

Anmuth ranks No. 832 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of about 9.40%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

#3139. Review: Aqara W200 supports Adaptive Temperature in HomeKit at a great price

Earlier this year, my wife and I bought our first house. Along with all the other exciting things, it’s also let me spend a lot of time testing new smart home gear.

One of the most important and useful smart home accessories is a smart thermostat. Six months ago, I installed the Aqara Smart Thermostat W200, and it’s been a fantastic addition to our smart home setup … especially because it supports Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature. Here’s how it works.

Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward. I’d previously installed various Ecobee thermostats. The trickiest part this time was learning the intricacies of the new house itself, which the Aqara app did a good job of guiding me through.

I used the Aqara app for the installation and setup, like choosing an interface design for the thermostat’s display itself. But after that, I closed the app and haven’t opened it since. Everything now is managed through the Apple Home app, and I appreciate that the Aqara app lets me do this without any pushback. It doesn’t try to pull me back into it to sell me a subscription or show me ads.

This matters because the Aqara app is nothing to write home about. It has a lot of settings, but I don’t think it’s particularly elegant or user-friendly. You can choose from a small collection of different screensavers. The thermostat’s interface is similar to the app in that it’s very utilitarian, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing for quick manual temperature adjustments.

The Aqara W200 also has a mmWave radar sensor that detects your presence. When you walk up to it, that sensor detects your approach and the screensaver automatically goes away to reveal the controls. It’s also exposed to HomeKit and can trigger automations. Unfortunately, this isn’t particularly useful for me because of the thermostat’s awkward location.

The Aqara W200’s build quality is good enough. It’s primarily made of plastic, unlike higher-end smart thermostats that feature metal housing, so it doesn’t look super premium on your wall. It has a responsive 4-inch touchscreen. It has a small footprint overall, so you’ll likely need the included back trim plate if your previous thermostat required a larger opening in the wall.

The standout feature of the Aqara W200, though, is its support for Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature, which debuted as part of iOS 26. As of right now, the Aqara W200 is the only thermostat with Adaptive Temperature support available, though two more are coming next year as part of Apple’s new Home Collection suite.

Adaptive Temperature is Apple’s feature that will automatically adjust your thermostat’s temperature based on your preferences. It uses your location and the location of other home members to determine when to adjust the thermostat.

Once you enable Adaptive Temperature, you set your ideal temperature range for the following states:

My wife and I set our preferred temperature ranges for each scenario. I particularly appreciate the ability to set a different range for night, since we like it noticeably colder overnight than during the day.

After that setup process, Adaptive Temperature has worked in the background without any involvement from us. It passively uses all the information on our iPhones to make its decision.

“Your iPhone uses on-device intelligence to predict when you’re on your way home to bring it to the correct temperature by the time you get there, and adjusts the thermostat to save energy when you are far away from home,” Apple explains.

Adaptive Temperature uses your iPhone and other home members’ devices to determine when to adjust the temperature. “Home can learn daily routines to predict when you’re likely to arrive and adjust the temperature for you,” Apple says. This includes things like your calendar events.

I can count on one hand the number of times we’ve had to manually adjust the thermostat since installing the W200, and most of those times were because we had guests with different preferences than ours.

Honestly, I thought I wrote this post months ago, but I guess it slipped my mind. I actually think there’s a pretty simple explanation for that, though. I installed the W200, enabled Adaptive Temperature in the Apple Home app, and haven’t thought about it since.

I think that’s a great endorsement of the Aqara W200 as a product. When I build a smart home, I want accessories that I can install, benefit from the “smarts” of, and never have to think about. That’s why I’ve also come to appreciate Lutron, which I’ve installed throughout my entire house. The Aqara W200 falls into that same bucket.

Between the Smart Thermostat W200 and UWB Smart Lock U400 (full review), Aqara powers two key pillars of my smart home, and I’ve been incredibly impressed with both.

The Aqara Smart Thermostat W200 is also very reasonably priced. It retails for $159.99, but is currently on sale for $119.99.

#3137. OpenAI countersues Apple, alleging trade secret theft and supplier threats; Apple responds

OpenAI has countersued Apple, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets and threatening suppliers working on its upcoming devices. The filing escalates a legal fight that began with Apple’s lawsuit against OpenAI in July.

OpenAI has launched a new legal action against Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers, in an effort to “compete unfairly by any means available”.

The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit in a California court on Friday, striking back after the iPhone maker accused the AI lab of stealing top-secret information this summer.

According to the report, OpenAI alleges Apple is “coercing and threatening” suppliers working with the ChatGPT maker. Its hardware ambitions include new personal devices following last year’s acquisition of Jony Ive’s “io” firm.

The complaint also claims Apple encouraged employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud accounts. OpenAI has previously characterized Apple’s case as an attempt to stop it from hiring Apple employees.

Apple’s original lawsuit names OpenAI, io Products, and former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan. Tan previously led iPhone and Apple Watch product design at Apple.

Apple alleges confidential engineering information and hardware development details were taken to benefit OpenAI’s consumer device efforts. OpenAI has disputed those allegations.

The new action also follows OpenAI’s October claim that an employee who returned to Apple sent more than 100 confidential files about unreleased OpenAI hardware to personal accounts. Those files allegedly included device images, engineering data, and supplier information.

Apple responded at the time that its investigation had not located OpenAI confidential information. The company said it requested more specific information to continue searching and would work with OpenAI to investigate the allegations.

Meanwhile, Apple has sought a preliminary injunction to prevent further use of its alleged trade secrets and won expanded access to evidence during discovery.

Apple’s original case is scheduled to go to trial on July 19, 2027.

Following publication, Apple shared the following statement with 9to5Mac:

“This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.”

#3136. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3133. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.
