#3132. How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons

The Europa Clipper will probe below the frozen surface for possible habitats for life

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA's Europa Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's icy moon in the 2030s.

On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper.

Tim Larson Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter?

Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy. It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter.

The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly?

Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys.

We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera.

The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)?

Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible.

How are Europa Clipper’s electronics different from other probes?

Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault—everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts). To get our usual factor-of-two margin, we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads.

That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that.

How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime?

Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3131. HomeKit Weekly: Meross’s new presence sensor splits a room into three zones for Apple Home

Presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that. They don’t tell it where in the room you are, though. That’s why these types of automations end up being all-or-nothing type things: you walk into a room, and every light comes on at full brightness, whether you came in to read at your desk or to grab something off the counter. The Meross MS605 splits its detection range into three distance zones, and each of them shows up in Apple Home as its own presence sensor so you can build automations around them.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

You’ll set the zones in the Meross iPhone app during setup, choosing a distance for each. Once the Meross MS605 is in Apple Home (via Matter), all three appear as separate presence sensors, and you can build automations for each individually. If you only want two, disable the third in the Meross app, and it disappears from the Home app as well.

A bathroom is the obvious use case here for early mornings. Set the far zone to turn a lamp on at 5% and the near zone to bring up an overhead light, etc.

The same idea works anywhere the room has more than one job. A hallway can light the path dim from the far zone, then go to 100% when you get close. An office can keep the overheads on while you’re anywhere in the room and turn on the desk lamp when you actually sit down as well. I find it incredibly useful for overall dimming, though.

The Meross MS605 uses mmWave radar and PIR together, which is the current best practice for presence detection. Meross says the radar picks up micro-movement, so it knows you’re there when you’re sitting still, and the PIR filters out things that move but aren’t warm, like curtains and a robot vacuum. There’s also a radar-only setting if you want it as well.

Range is up to about 20 feet for motion and 13 feet for presence, with each zone configurable within those limits. There’s a built-in light sensor, too, so you can gate your lighting automations based on actual room brightness instead of guessing when you’ll want it with a sunset/sunrise trigger.

The Meross MS605 is IP67-rated and operates from -4 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, so a covered porch, a garage, or a basement is all fair game for placing the sensor.

The initial setup runs via the Meross app over Bluetooth, and the app is required afterward. Zones, sensitivity, presence-and-absence timing, recalibration, and firmware updates all live in it. Day-to-day control and automation happen in Apple Home, but anything you want to tune requires going back.

One minor thing to know before you mount somewhere hard to reach: changing settings over Bluetooth requires pressing a physical button on top of the sensor, so keep that in mind when configuring your settings and initially placing it.

The Meross MS605 unlocks some unique use cases with its three zones. Three zones from one sensor is a new automation tool, and the IP67 rating means you can put it in places other presence sensors can’t go. It’s powered by a CR123A battery, which is included in the box.

Over the last two years I've been testing AR glasses, or display glasses to be more accurate. If you haven't worn a pair, at their most basic level these glasses include a secondary lens that projects a massive display on the glasses.

I've traveled, gamed, and just watched movies in bed with these glasses. My colleague Anthony Spadafora managed to combine all three when he spent a weekend in the world of GTA 6 using a pair of AR glasses. Trust me, it's totally immersive.

For the holiday season, many of the best smart glasses are on sale, and now's the time to dip your toes in. I've found options ranging from budget-friendly specs to top-of-the-line glasses that even offer some spatial computing.

RayNeo is the king of budget-friendly AR glasses while still offering excellent features and comfortable fits. Even the new GT Max, the company's high-end glasses, are still priced well-below similar offerings from Xreal and Viture.

Of the glasses highlighted here, the Air 4 Pro are the oldest (not that old), but they still hold up offering a 201-inch display and HDR10, something no other AR specs have. It's one of the reasons I recommend it over even the new GT glasses. They do feel budget but at $233, that's not too bad. In our RayNeo Air 4 Pro review we praised the included light blocked, vivid picture quality and they fit well.

The GT are RayNeo's newest budget option and they come with Dolby Vision. Like the Air 4 Pro they have an excellent display, comfortable fit and new steady/pinned modes for when you're traveling or sitting in one place for a while. They are a bit better than the Air 4 Pro, so it's up to you which one you think fits your style better. In my RayNeo GT review I found the GT has the best display among the $299 range display glasses.

RayNeo finally stepped into the high-end AR game with the GT Max and it shows with its huge 267-inch display, 59 degree field of view and native 3DoF support. They feel lighter thanks to the new prism optics and yet, they're still less expensive than other high-end models. These are a standout entry point for anyone looking to get into display glasses as we said in our RayNeo GT Max review.

Xreal just dropped its XR Aura glasses which truly are a shrunk down version of a VR headset. But those glasses aren't on sale and they're aren't cheap at over $1,000. Fortunately, Xreal makes other excellent AR glasses that are on sale from stylish budget options to high-end versions.

The oddly named xbx a01+ are Xreal's attempt at a budget-friendly pair of AR glasses. Sacrifices were made but these glasses are some of the only display specs that truly pass the pub test are actually stylish and fun to look at. That said, they're also lightweight, feature a bright 1600 nit display and can connect with most devices. As we said in our Xreal xbx ao1+ review, if you just want a simple pair of glasses that lets you play games and watch movies without straining your neck, the xbx have you.

Xreal just refreshed its top of the line AR glasses in October with better brightness, new AI HDR enhanceer, 60 fps 2D-to-3D conversion and new modes depending on what you're viewing from reading to movies. Xreal also redesigned the nosepad to be more comfortable and ergonomic. If you haven't tried the refresh or want to go big, try the 1 Pro+. I was really impressed in my Xreal 1 Pro+ testing.

If there's a rivalry in the world of AR glasses it's between Viture and Xreal. It's real back and forth between these two companies with neither one separating from the pack. Which means Viture makes great glasses that compete against the best of Xreal.

Out-of-the-box the Viture Beast give you some of the best picture quality we've seen with on-device tweaks and a separate software suite if you want. They're comfortable to wear and reliable performers. They're our top pick in our best of lists and as we said in our Viture Beast review, simply put these are the best money can buy right now.

No, the Viture Pro 2 aren't on sale but hands down these are my favorite budget-level AR glasses. They feature superior display tech, redesigned comfort and adjustability making them viable for more people. That's all coupled with a great 146-inch virtual screen that's super bright and sharp. #3128. This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer

Dinesh Rai’s role as Boston Children’s prompt engineer quickly outgrew its bounds

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist.

In his home office, Dinesh Rai splits his time between working with engineers and clinicians at Boston Children’s Hospital.

When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.

At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.

Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.

Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.

When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.

Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”

For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.

Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.

For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.

His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.

That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.

At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.

One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.

The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.

Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.

Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.

Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.

Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.

Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.

“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”

In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?

That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.

Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”

The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.

What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.

That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.

“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist focusing on technology.

#3127. Apple faces potential $80 million fine and App Store overhaul in Chile [U: Apple responds]

Chile’s national competition authority, Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases. Here are the details.

As reported by Reuters, Chile’s competition watchdog is seeking an $80 million fine against Apple, along with a court order requiring a series of changes to the company’s App Store policies.

In its complaint, the FNE says (translation ours):

The defendant has violated Article 3, paragraphs one and two, subsection (b), of Decree Law 211 by abusing its dominant position through practices that prevent, restrict, or hinder free competition, or have the potential to do so, in the markets for app distribution and the distribution of paid digital goods within apps, both on the iOS operating system nationwide, from at least 2019 to the present day.

The FNE goes on to say that Apple forbids both sideloading and alternative app marketplaces, requires app developers to exclusively use the company’s In-App Purchase system to sell digital goods and services within their apps, and restricts their ability to inform users about or direct them to alternative payment methods.

It then goes on to claim that “these anticompetitive practices have allowed the defendant to ensure that the App Store is the only channel for downloading apps,” adding that this “has led to a degradation of the consumer experience and allowed Apple to secure profits that it would not obtain without such practices.”

That includes Apple’s agreement with Brazil’s competition authority, the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, the Epic Games v. Apple ruling in Australia, regulatory and judicial developments in Japan, and the lifting of anti-steering restrictions in the US.

At one point, the FNE even suggests that Apple knowingly maintained anticompetitive practices in the country, despite regulatory and judicial developments elsewhere:

Furthermore, there is evidence suggesting that the defendant was aware of the unlawfulness of its conduct, given the existence of precedents in other jurisdictions involving facts similar to those alleged in this complaint, which demonstrate the anticompetitive nature of the alleged practices. Nevertheless, Apple decided to maintain its restrictions in Chile, as well as in other jurisdictions where it has not been compelled to remove them or has not agreed with the relevant authority to eliminate or modify them.

After presenting its case, the FNE asks Chile’s antitrust court to:

Additionally, the FNE asks the court to require Apple to implement these measures “in good faith, such that it may not impose any other technical or contractual restrictions, or commercial conditions, that undermine their purpose,” to cease the alleged anticompetitive practices, and to cover the legal costs of the proceedings.

It also leaves room for the court to impose any additional measures it deems appropriate, particularly those aimed at facilitating access to alternative channels for app distribution and the sale of digital goods.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and will update this post if the company responds.

You can read the FNE’s full complaint here (in Spanish).

Update, 8:20 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

We are aware of the request filed by FNE and will continue to cooperate with the authorities throughout this process. We designed the App Store to keep users safe and their information secure, and to give developers in Chile and around the world a trusted place to reach customers and grow their businesses. We will continue to advocate for users and developers on our platform.

Apple also expanded on its statement, arguing that it doesn’t hold a monopoly in any market worldwide, pointing to Android’s leading position in the global smartphone market.

The company also took issue with the FNE’s market definition, which it noted has been rejected by other courts and fails to account for competition from other app marketplaces, such as the Google Play Store, Samsung Galaxy Store, Huawei AppGallery, in addition to PC and gaming console storefronts.

Regarding its IAP system, Apple highlighted its fraud-prevention measures, which it said blocked more than $2.2 billion in potentially fraudulent transactions in 2025 alone, as well as features such as subscription management, refund support, and parental controls via Ask to Buy.

Finally, Apple argued that requiring it to allow developers to direct users to external payment systems would leave users more exposed to scams and misleading pricing practices, and would also make it possible to circumvent certain parental controls.

#3124. MacWhisper now remembers speakers’ voices across recordings

Dutch developer Jordi Bruin rolled out an update to his excellent transcription app MacWhisper this week with a much-requested feature: the ability to automatically identify previously named speakers in new recordings. Here are the details.

I’ve written multiple times in the past couple of years about how MacWhisper has become an integral part of my podcast post-production workflow for show notes, episode descriptions, and more.

Which is why I’ve followed the app’s development very closely, and Jordi’s efforts to make it an increasingly powerful tool for casual and power users alike.

In the last few months alone, MacWhisper got a completely redesigned transcript editor, real-time meeting transcription, significantly improved speaker detection, deeper integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Spotlight, and support for multiple new transcription models.

This week, MacWhisper got updated to version 16, packing several improvements, chief among them the ability to recognize speakers based on their voices in previous transcripts.

Until now, while MacWhisper could distinguish between different speakers in a recording (a process known as speaker diarization), users still had to assign names to each new transcription manually. With MacWhisper 16, that is no longer necessarily the case.

Now, MacWhisper creates a set of voiceprints for the speakers users have previously identified, and uses them as a reference when processing new recordings. Depending on the confidence level of a match, MacWhisper will either automatically assign the speaker’s name or ask the user to confirm their identity.

According to Bruin, as users transcribe more recordings featuring the same people, MacWhisper gets better at recognizing their voices. All voiceprint processing and storage happen on-device, which is a great touch.

The feature also works with existing transcripts, which is fantastic for longtime MacWhisper users such as myself. A new Voice Recognition section in the app’s settings lets users generate voiceprints from existing transcripts, clear a speaker’s stored voice data, or turn the feature off altogether.

Importantly, voice recognition also works with live meeting transcriptions, although automatic name assignments happen once the meeting ends.

The new feature requires a MacWhisper Pro license, an Apple silicon Mac, and on-device transcription with speaker detection enabled.

It's the weekend after Thanksgiving, and we're nursing a collective food coma. It's the perfect time to plop down on the couch and put on a movie, but which one threatens to make or break your night. Narrowing down what to watch is a chore, and one I hope to help you skip with this comprehensive guide to the best new movies on streaming.

Leading the pack this week is a double feature on paid video-on-demand platforms: 1) the Nathan Fielder documentary everyone and their mom can't stop talking about and 2) the horniest movie I've seen in a while starring Peter Dinklage and Olivia Colman at her most unhinged since "The Favorite."

Over on Netflix, you'll find a new World War II movie about football from the director of "Friday Night Lights." HBO Max just got a family friendly adventure led by Andrew Garfield as a dad you can't help but root for. And "Reacher" star Alan Ritchson teams up with Owen Wilson in an action thriller on Hulu.

So without further ado, let's dive into the best new movies on streaming this weekend.

You can now stream Nathan Fielder's fascinating and at times frustrating documentary "You Can See Everything" from the comfort of your couch, and pay at least $20 for the privilege. It's a sure bet for Best Documentary at the 2027 Oscars with a remarkable 97% on Rotten Tomatoes. If it were me, I'd wait until it comes to HBO Max in early 2027 — and save your hard-earned cash for the next entry in this list.

In our "You Can See Everything" review, my colleague called it "a bold, innovative documentary from alt-comedy creator Nathan Fielder and nonfiction filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, offering a fascinating look at convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes." The notorious tech-industry scammer has an acute allergy to self-reflection and proves nearly as manipulative as Fielder himself as the two get closer with the clock ticking down to her prison sentence.

Buy or rent "You Can See Everything" on Amazon now

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Now if you're dead set on relieving yourself of $25 to "own" a movie, "Wicker" is the clear choice for the horniest among us. I saw this in theaters with the girlies, and oh, how we cackled. Olivia Colman is as darling as ever as the prickly fisherwoman, who shows up at the local basket weaver's (Peter Dinklage) door with a weird ask. One wicker husband, coming up!

Alexander Skarsgård is uncanny and charming as her (and the town's) new obsession. Until things go sideways once a little wicker baby shows up...with another woman. "Wicker" is a delightfully horny time, theatrical as all get out, and Dinklage is given leave to soliloquy to his hearts' content. What more could you ask for to wile away a chilly weekend evening?

I'm not the biggest WWII movie buff, but my husband's excited to queue this one up if he can take a break from his emotional support WWII documentaries. A new war drama based on Buzz Bissinger’s nonfiction book of the same name, "The Mosquito Bowl" follows four college football stars who join the swell of promising young lads enlisting in the United States Marine Corps after Pearl Harbor.

With the Battle of Okinawa on the horizon, the guys — played by Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis — stage a football game that would become known as "The Mosquito Bowl" that proves a welcome break from the daily horror of the frontlines. "Friday Night Lights" and "Lone Survivor" director Peter Berg is at the helm of this one, so you know you're in for something memorable, at the very least.

Watch "The Magic Faraway Tree" on HBO Max now

"Reacher" star Alan Ritchson has been popping up everywhere lately. He joins forces with Owen Wilson in Hulu's latest action-comedy "Runner" where he gets plenty of opportunities to throw a punch. Ritchson stars as Hank Malone, a former soldier thrown into a frantic race against the clock when a medical delivery lands him squarely in the crosshairs of a ruthless cartel. With an innocent child's life hanging in the balance, Hank's determined to get his cargo where it needs to go before it's too late.

Owen Wilson co-stars as his partner, alongside Rodrigo Santoro as a cartel member and Leila George, with Scott Waugh of "Need for Speed" and "Expend4bles" fame in the director's chair. "Reacher's" really been on a downward trend since season one, but Ritchson and Wilson play off each other well enough in this breezy popcorn watch. And that's exactly the kind of thing that's calling my name after inhaling Thanksgiving dinner.

#3122. Apple claims six of China’s 10 bestselling smartphones during Singles’ Day

Counterpoint Research says Apple led smartphone sales in China during this year’s Double 11 shopping festival (also known as Singles’ Day), despite a broader slump in smartphone demand. Here are the details.

Last year, Counterpoint Research found that during China’s Double 11 shopping period, strong demand for the iPhone 17 lineup helped drive a 3% year-over-year increase in smartphone sales in the country.

This year, Apple once again came out on top, though rising smartphone prices and limited promotional discounts weighed on overall consumer demand.

According to the report, Apple saw an 8% year-over-year decline in iPhone sales during the promotional period. Still, compared with the market-wide 17% drop, Apple fared considerably better than most of its competitors.

Furthermore, Apple accounted for six of the 10 bestselling smartphone models during the promotional period, including all five of the top spots.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max topped the ranking, while the newly launched iPhone Duo came in ninth despite going on sale only on October 23, nearly two weeks after the shopping festival kicked off on October 12.

Counterpoint also noted that Huawei “was the only major OEM to record growth, up 29% YoY, driven mainly by the Enjoy 90 Pro Max and Pura X View, with the new Enjoy 100 series providing an additional boost.” The Enjoy 90 Pro Max was the only Huawei model to make the top 10, coming in sixth.

#3121. Top Wall Street analysts are upbeat about the prospects for these 3 stocks

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3119. WhatsApp announces travel eSIMs, tests view-once texts and a cleaner interface

In addition to officially announcing support for in-app travel eSIM purchases, WhatsApp is now reportedly testing two new features on iOS. Here are the details.

WhatsApp yesterday announced that iPhone and Android users will soon be able to purchase and install travel eSIMs directly from the app.

According to the company, the feature will allow users to get a mobile data plan for international travel with just a few taps, without having to leave WhatsApp, while continuing to use the messaging service with their existing phone number.

To make this possible, we’re working with e-SIM providers and telco partners including Jio, Smart Axiata, Smart Communications, Verizon and others, and we’ll begin rolling this out in select countries soon. You’ll see it right in the app when it’s available for you.

Additionally, WABetaInfo reported this week that users running WhatsApp’s TestFlight beta are starting to see the option to send view-once text messages, extending a feature that is already available for photos, videos, and voice messages.

WABetaInfo noted that after long-pressing the send button, users who have access to the new feature can select between scheduling the message and sending it as a view-once message.

Recipients can then tap the message to read it in a separate interface, with WhatsApp blocking screenshots, screen recordings, copying, and forwarding. Once the recipient closes the message, neither party can access its contents again.

In another test rolling out to iPhone beta users, WhatsApp is making a slight change to the app’s tab bar, removing the text labels that appear below each icon while preserving its existing Liquid Glass design.

With the latest update, the text labels within the tab bar are no longer visible. The tab bar now shows icons for Updates, Calls, Contacts, Chats, and You without any labels. This makes the tab bar more compact since the app no longer needs to reserve more space for its labels. WhatsApp makes icons with the tab bar clear and recognizable, so users can still identify every tab immediately.

As is usually the case with WhatsApp beta features, there is no telling when (or if) these two changes will make their way to the public version of the app.

To learn more about WhatsApp’s upcoming travel eSIM feature, follow this link. For WABetaInfo’s coverage of the two beta features, see here and here.

If you regularly wake up feeling stiff, notice your hips tightening after sitting for too long, or find that everyday movements leave you feeling achy, it might be time to pay attention to your mobility. While some changes in flexibility and joint movement are a natural part of aging, aches, stiffness and tension don't have to become something you put up with.

One of the best ways to keep your body moving comfortably is to make mobility work a priority. Gentle, controlled movements take your joints through their range of motion, help maintain flexibility and strengthen the muscles that support everyday movement. You don't need to spend hours stretching to see the benefits — a short routine practised regularly can be a better way to build the habit.

With that in mind, I asked Dr. Gaby Van Sickle, physical therapist and co-founder of Functional Physical Therapy, to share a 10-minute mobility workout she recommends to her clients. The routine combines simple movements to keep your hips, knees and ankles moving, build lower-body strength and support the balance and coordination we rely on as we age.

So, if you're looking for a practical way to ease stiffness and keep those everyday aches and pains at bay, here's how to fit 10 minutes of mobility into your day.

Why: Van Sickle recommends starting with walking because it’s the ideal way to prepare the body for movement. “It gradually increases blood flow to the muscles, and encourages movement through the hips, knees, ankles, and spine,” she says. “It’ll also help reduce the sensation of stiffness before beginning more targeted mobility exercises.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 4-6 per move in each direction

Time: 1 minute Reps: 10 in each direction

Why: Shoulder rolls are the ideal addition to your longevity toolkit. “They help improve mobility through the shoulders and upper back, which makes movements like reaching overhead and getting dressed easier,” Van Sickle says. Over time, they’ll help ease aching in the shoulders and neck.

Why: Neck and lower back stiffness are common, and it’s usually caused by too much pressure or tension in this area. “Thoracic rotations help relieve this by distributing movement throughout the trunk,” Van Sickle explains.

Why: These are great to do after prolonged periods of sitting, as they “promote movement through the spine and pelvis, helping to reduce any stiffness.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 8-10 of each movement per leg

Why: Van Sickle recommends these moves frequently to her clients because they promote active hip mobility while strengthening the gluteal muscles. Keeping the hips mobile and the surrounding muscles strong can help reduce feelings of stiffness and make everyday movements, like walking and stepping to the side, feel more comfortable.

Why: “This is a functional movement that promotes mobility and strength through the core, hips, knees, and ankles,” Van Sickle says. Staying active in these areas helps reduce stiffness in the lower body.

Why: Stiff ankles and tight lower-leg muscles can make walking feel less comfortable. Practicing calf raises and toe raises moves the ankle in both directions while strengthening the muscles around it, which will help support a smoother, more comfortable stride.

Time: 1 minute Reps: 15-30 marches per leg

Why: Standing marches gently move the hips and knees while encouraging you to shift your weight from one leg to the other. “It’s about keeping the lower body moving to ease feelings of stiffness after periods of sitting or inactivity,” Van Sickle advocates.

If aches, stiffness and tension are making everyday movement feel more difficult, a regular mobility routine can help. These exercises gently move your hips, knees and ankles through their range of motion while strengthening the muscles that support your joints, helping you maintain the mobility, balance and strength you need as you age.

The key is consistency, rather than pushing yourself to do more. Try setting aside 10 minutes each day to work through the routine, moving slowly and staying within a comfortable range of motion. Over time, a regular practice can help you feel less stiff after periods of inactivity and more confident with everyday movements.

You don't have to write a single line of code to appreciate what it can do

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Claude Code might sound like something exclusively reserved for software engineers, but you don't need to know a single programming language to put Anthropic's AI agent to work.

While Claude is great for answering questions, brainstorming ideas and writing emails, Claude Code can work directly with files on your computer, execute commands and tackle projects that would otherwise require several different apps.

The beauty of Claude Code is that you can describe what you want done in plain English and let the AI handle the technical side. From tackling an embarrassingly messy Downloads folder to making sense of years of family photos, here are seven surprisingly practical ways to use Claude Code that have nothing to do with programming, along with the prompts to get started.

If your Downloads folder has become a digital junk drawer filled with screenshots, PDFs, receipts and files you don't even remember downloading, Claude Code can help you sort through the mess.

Rather than manually opening every file and figuring out where it belongs, you can ask Claude to categorize documents, suggest more descriptive file names and organize copies into subfolders.

What makes this particularly useful is that Claude Code can do the actual organizational work rather than simply recommend a folder structure for you to create yourself.

Prompt: Review the files in this folder and organize them into meaningful categories based on their contents. Identify potential duplicates and suggest descriptive file names. Show me your proposed organization before making any changes. Do not delete or overwrite anything.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Most banking apps tell you how much you've spent, but they don't necessarily give you the level of detail you want about your spending habits.

Download a CSV of your transactions, remove sensitive personal and account information and give Claude Code a copy. You can ask it to categorize expenses, identify recurring subscriptions and create a customized spreadsheet with charts that visualize your spending.

You could even have Claude identify subscriptions that have gone up in price or calculate how much you're spending on takeout compared to groceries.

Instead of paying for another budgeting app, you can create a financial dashboard tailored to the information you actually care about.

Prompt: Analyze this CSV of my transactions. Categorize my spending, identify recurring subscriptions, flag unusual expenses and create an Excel dashboard with monthly spending trends and potential savings. Do not modify the original file or invent missing information.

Between screenshots, phone backups and photos transferred from old devices, it's surprisingly easy to accumulate thousands of poorly organized images.

Claude Code can use available image metadata to sort photos by date, identify exact duplicates and create a more manageable folder structure without requiring you to drag and drop hundreds of files.

You can also ask it to separate screenshots from camera photos where possible, making it easier to find the pictures you actually want to keep.

I'd recommend starting with a small batch of copied photos before tackling your entire collection.

Prompt: Review the photos in this folder and use available metadata to organize copies by year and month. Identify exact duplicates and screenshots. Flag photos with missing dates rather than guessing. Preserve every original image and create a summary of what you've organized.

As a mom of three, I know how quickly school newsletters, sports schedules, permission slips and appointment reminders can pile up. Keeping track of everything often means digging through multiple emails and attachments just to figure out what's happening next week.

Save those documents in a dedicated folder and ask Claude Code to extract important dates, deadlines, locations and reminders.

The AI can generate an .ics calendar file that you can review and import into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook. That saves you from having to manually create an event for every soccer practice, school concert or early dismissal.

Prompt: Review all the documents in this folder and extract important dates, deadlines, appointments and events. Create a chronological schedule and an importable .ics calendar file. Include locations and relevant notes. Flag conflicting or ambiguous dates for my review rather than making assumptions.

Before you spend money on additional cloud storage or an external hard drive, it might be worth finding out what's actually eating up space on your computer.

Claude Code can examine selected folders, identify unusually large files, locate exact duplicates and generate a report showing where you could potentially reclaim storage.

You could discover everything from forgotten video exports to multiple copies of the same large presentation. You can also ask Claude to break down its findings in plain English so you know what you're looking at before deciding what to remove.

The key here is to have Claude investigate rather than automatically delete anything.

Prompt: Perform a read-only storage audit of this folder. Identify the largest files, exact duplicates, old downloads and unusually large subfolders. Create a report showing potential storage savings and explain which files I should review manually. Do not delete, move or modify anything.

If your favorite recipes are scattered across screenshots, Word documents, PDFs and random text files, Claude Code can help you turn them into something you might actually use.

Give Claude a folder containing your recipes and ask it to extract the ingredients, standardize the formatting and categorize everything into a collection. You can even have it produce a printable PDF cookbook with a cover and table of contents.

For something more personal, you could turn a collection of family recipes into a homemade cookbook to give relatives for the holidays.

Prompt: Turn the recipes in this folder into a professionally formatted PDF cookbook. Organize them by meal type, create a table of contents and standardize ingredient lists and instructions. Preserve the original measurements and flag any missing information instead of inventing it.

Creating a home inventory is one of those things most of us know we should do but never quite get around to.

Having an organized record of your belongings, receipts and warranties could make life considerably easier when you need to file an insurance claim, replace an appliance or find out whether something is still under warranty.

Claude Code can work through a collection of receipts, product manuals and photos to create a home inventory spreadsheet. It can also organize copies of supporting documents so they're easier to find when you need them.

You could even ask Claude to create a separate maintenance schedule for household appliances based on their instruction manuals.

Prompt: Review the receipts, manuals and product photos in this folder. Create a home inventory spreadsheet with product names, model numbers, purchase dates, prices, warranty information and links to supporting files. Mark anything you cannot verify as unknown. Preserve all original documents.

What makes Claude Code interesting beyond programming is its ability to bridge the gap between getting advice from an AI chatbot and actually getting something done.

Of course, giving an AI agent access to your computer comes with risks. I recommend starting with a dedicated folder containing copies of your documents, reviewing permission requests carefully and keeping backups of anything important. Always double-check the finished results, particularly when dealing with financial information or important deadlines.

#3112. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3111. Pfizer's 6% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?

Pfizer is facing down big patent expirations, but that's pretty normal in the drug sector.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST

AbbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%. But it is important to recognize that the average drug company's yield is only 1.3% and the broader market's yield is just 1%, so AbbVie's yield isn't exactly small. Here's why conservative dividend investors wouldn't be making a mistake by buying AbbVie, but if you can handle a little uncertainty, Pfizer's much higher yield may end up being the better option.

One of the big positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King. That means that the company has increased its dividend annually for 50+ consecutive years (53 to be specific), which is not something that happens by accident. It requires a strong business model that is executed well in both good and bad markets. The only problem here is that AbbVie hasn't actually existed for 50 years. It was created in 2013 when it was spun off from Abbott Laboratories (ABT +0.07%). It retained Abbott's dividend record and then, to AbbVie's credit, continued to raise its dividend each year.

Still, it probably isn't appropriate to give AbbVie full credit for its Dividend King status. You should pay extra attention to its actual business, which is well-run and fairly well-positioned. It has strong positions in immunology and oncology. Meanwhile, the drug maker's aesthetics business doesn't face the same patent risks as other drug niches because brand names are important differentiators. As a business, it is highly desirable.

There's just one small problem: the stock isn't cheap. Its price-to-sales ratio is 7.9x compared to a five-year average of 5.4x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 50x compared to a five-year average of 41x. You are paying full fair, if not more, for the stock's above-average yield.

That's where Pfizer starts to look relatively attractive. Not only is its dividend yield likely to be highly attractive to income seekers, but the stock is also much cheaper than AbbVie. Pfizer's 2.5x P/S ratio is in line with its five-year average and far lower than AbbVie's 7.9x. Pfizer's P/E ratio is 40x, which is biased higher by one-time charges and still lower than AbbVie's 50x. If you use the $3.00 per share midpoint of Pfizer's 2026 adjusted earnings guidance, the P/E is around 10x. That's below the stock's nearly 14x five-year average.

A big yield from a cheap stock will likely have more appeal than a smaller yield from an expensive stock for most investors. But there are issues to consider, most notably Pfizer's upcoming patent expirations in 2028 (Eliquis) and 2031 (Vyndamax). Those are big deals and will likely result in a substantial decline in revenues and earnings. The thing is, patent expirations are entirely normal in the pharmaceutical sector. Pfizer is working hard to develop new drugs to offset the hit, but sometimes the timing doesn't perfectly align.

Still, given the company's strong history, which dates back to the mid-1800s, it seems highly likely that it will manage this patent expiration cycle, just as it has many times before. As for the dividend, the company is publicly supportive of it and continues to tell investors that its long-term goal is to grow the payment. And even if there were a 50% dividend cut, which seems like a reasonable worst-case scenario, the yield would still be higher than AbbVie's 2.3%.

If you are a risk-averse investor who simply can't tolerate any kind of uncertainty, AbbVie is a perfectly fine, though perhaps expensive, stock to buy. However, Pfizer's higher yield and more attractive valuation will probably make it a better option, assuming you believe it can muddle through its patent-expiration issues, as it has many times before. Indeed, the risk-versus-reward balance is likely tilted toward reward for long-term dividend investors.

#3110. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. #3107. CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Packages Could Be at Risk of Holiday Porch Theft

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

US adults have an average package value of $276.24, yet one-fifth don't use security devices due to costs.

Big holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, are here, but before you click ‘buy,’ make sure you have a plan to protect your package from porch pirates.

CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent thefts. This year, the average package value is $276.24, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

But leaving your packages up for grabs could be a big risk — especially when thieves know holiday gifts are being delivered. On the other hand, some bad actors don’t seem to mind being caught in the act on home security cameras, so are they really enough to deter bad actors? And what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other issues like break-ins,” said CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma said that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and new porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

So while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to plan how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

Lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

“I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” said Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

Among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

You shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

“Delivery boxes have reached a new level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” said Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”

If you don’t want to install a new security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

“Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” said Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”

If you’re looking for a camera that’s off-the-grid, consider the Arlo Go 2. It’s an LTE camera, so it uses a cellular data connection instead of Wi-Fi. It still finds a signal, supports app operation and live video viewing. If you’re looking for a power-over-Ethernet camera that uses a cable connection, the Reolink Duo 3 is a good choice.

Among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

“Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” said Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

The tool changer technology also allows you to mix different materials with less of a fuss, so you can use a typical rigid plastic and something like a flexible rubber in a single pass without stopping. It can switch between different nozzle sizes in one job. You can switch between  0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm midprint.

The P3C ships with an integrated sealed AMS 3P filament management system that can store up to seven spools, each of which is on an independent feed path to the printer. You can also connect up to four external AMS units, supporting up to 22 colors.

The P3C is more than just a 3D printer. The Swaptek system supports interchangeable craft tools, letting you cut, draw or emboss on materials.

Bambu Lab also included a few features that make the P3C more approachable to newcomers. The P3C provides full-auto calibration, automatically aligning nozzle offsets and multi-tool heads so you don’t have to do it yourself. There’s also a built-in AI monitoring system that can detect issues like nozzle clogs and purge-bin jams early on. A new health management system will no longer spit out vague or obscure errors when something goes wrong. Instead, the new system will explain the issue in plain language and provide step-by-step troubleshooting right on the screen.

CNET’s 3D printing expert, James Bricknell, hasn’t been able to test Bambu Labs’ latest model yet but is excited about it. “While the P3C didn’t arrive in time for a hands-on, it’s built with the same design language and hardware support as the recently released H3C. If it is anywhere near as good, and I think that’s likely, it’ll be at the top of any serious 3D printing enthusiast’s wish list.”

The P3C 3D printer AMS combo is available now worldwide for $1,149. The combo includes the printer, AMS 3P as well as 5 0.4mm standard PrintTools. Two slots are left open for you to customize. This combo option comes with virtually everything you need to get started printing your works of art and more.
