#3101. A Human and an AI Model (Apparently) Solved the Riemann Hypothesis: What it Means for Future of Math

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The AI-assisted proof is 250,000 pages long, and mathematicians are trying to understand what it says.

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of math’s oldest and most famous unsolved problems. It was originally put forward as a problem in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, and professional and amateur mathematicians alike have made thousands of attempts to solve it. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge has apparently solved the problem with the help of AI, showing that in the battle of humans versus AI, the real winner might be both of them working together.

Alpöge made the announcement on Friday in a four-page document (PDF) on his personal web page.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge said in the announcement. “In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.”

The actual hypothesis itself isn’t the biggest deal since all it does is make it easier to see the distribution of prime numbers. However, math didn’t come to a screeching halt just because the hypothesis hadn’t been proven. There are hundreds of other math theorems along with algorithms and cryptographic encryption methods that operate based on the assumption that the Riemann Hypothesis is true.

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Problems for this very reason. If Alpöge really did solve the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude’s help, it would remove a metaphorical logjam that’s been gumming up the works for over a century and a half. Most of those hundreds of math theorems would be proven as true overnight, and all of those algorithms and encryption methods would be validated. That would make solving the Riemann Hypothesis one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in history.

“It is certainly an exciting time,” Paul Milewski, head of the department of mathematics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET. “The Riemann Hypothesis (or any big theorem) is often not the ‘goal’ of mathematics. They are set up as grand challenges that require the development of new tools, new results along the way and new understanding. It is the ‘voyage’ and not the destination that matters the most.”

As such, the mathematics community wasted no time testing the proof to see whether it was true. Two groups — Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative — independently verified the proof, with many other researchers running their own tests and coming to the same conclusion.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on the achievement,” the two groups said in a joint statement on Saturday.

This is certainly an exciting discovery, but it’s not without its obstacles. Alpöge’s proof was a staggering 250,000 pages of some of the most complex math ever written by a human or a machine. Alpöge provided 17 million lines of Lean code, a programming language specifically made for writing and checking proofs, and that’s how researchers were able to check the work and show it to be true.

The problem is that the average novel is about 300 pages, and that means that Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is approximately 833 novels’ worth of complex math. For reference, the longest work ever produced is World-2023, which holds the Guinness World Record at 100,100 pages. That book is 19 feet tall, and Alpöge’s proof is two and a half times longer.

Despite the logic being verified as true through Lean code, Alpöge still has a major problem. So far, none of the mathematicians or researchers who have attempted to read it have been able to understand what it says.

“I do not understand, and I suspect no human completely understands,” Jon Keating, professor of mathematical physics at the University of Oxford, said in a Numberphile YouTube video. “When I look at that, I’m completely in awe and in wonderment.”

For the problem to be fully solved, the proof has to be read, analyzed and simplified so that it can be translated into readable mathematics, which Alpöge says in his announcement that he’s in the process of doing. All of this has to be done so that Alpöge can publish it in a peer-reviewed journal in such a way that his peers can actually read it. It is only after the mathematics community scrutinizes and accepts Alpöge’s proof that it is considered fully solved.

Aside from being nigh unreadable to humans, Alpöge has otherwise avoided the kinds of drama that other AI-assisted discoveries have faced in 2026.

OpenAI had to backtrack on its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem, which is another Millennium Problem, after the company couldn’t rule out that the AI models it used had access to data from other researchers. Somewhat ironically, one of those mathematicians whose work OpenAI may have  — knowingly or unknowingly — borrowed from was Levent Alpöge, as he and others were pretty close to solving the problem on their own.

Similarly, Claude was credited with finding a new novel enzyme that humans had never seen before. The problem is that computational biologist Mario Rodríguez Mestre had seen this enzyme before and was using Claude to study it further, so it’s uncertain if Claude actually found it independently or used data from Mestre’s research to find it.

The heavy assistance from AI has been met with mostly positive reactions, with most researchers agreeing that the AI usage is justified provided that the proof is proven to be true through peer review. Since no one was particularly close to solving the Riemann Hypothesis, there haven’t been any accusations of Alpöge or Claude stealing work like those prior examples. By and large, most mathematicians are excited about the discovery.

“Even before this, we have seen the power of AI, and this shows that AI trained on hundreds of years of human mathematics can perform amazing tasks,” said Penn State’s Milewski. “I would add that AI didn’t come up with the Riemann Hypothesis, nor did most of the work to prove it, and AI probably doesn’t ‘know’ why it was invented or why it’s important.”

CNET spoke with a few professors about this, and they all echoed Milewski’s sentiment, stating that AI was trained with centuries of human mathematical achievement, so a win for AI is a win for humans too. Jeffrey Lagarias, a professor of mathematics at the University of Michigan, told CNET that “I don’t think this particular proof would have been found without AI.”

Prasad Tetali, head of the department of mathematical sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, said: “It is easy to overestimate the role of AI, and underappreciate decades of human mathematician work that went into it. The AI here is really standing tall and wide on the shoulders of generations of human giants.”

On the AI side of things, influencers are attempting to use the news to hype up the capabilities of AI. Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang said in a post on X that solving the Riemann Hypothesis was a sign that AI superintelligence was close at hand and that humanity should be terrified of the “alien mind that we don’t understand.”

AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky likened the whole thing to a company making enriched uranium that’ll one day result in the end of the human species.

These warnings are hard to take seriously when one considers that Anthropic tried to make Claude solve the Riemann Hypothesis by itself back in August. Claude came up with some cool ideas but ultimately failed to solve the problem alone. For the time being, AI still needs a great deal of human guidance to make these massive discoveries, so the doom-and-gloom proselytizing comes off as a little premature.

To make things even more interesting, a competing Riemann Hypothesis proof was submitted by Alessandro Masullo just a few hours after Alpöge released his. This competing proof is 940 pages long, which is significantly shorter than Alpöge’s proof, and it was an all-human effort with no AI assistance. The proof is months in the making, with Masullo working with mathematician Brian Conrad to bring it up to spec before it hits peer review. When Alpöge posted his proof, Masullo and others thought it wise to submit theirs as well.

This started a “dueling proofs” storyline over the weekend, but it was short-lived. Shortly after Masullo’s proof was posted, multiple people found the types of flaws and omissions that often disprove Riemann Hypothesis proofs. Those issues are in the process of being corrected, and the proof is officially in mid-revision status.

Masullo kept the original proof posted (PDF) in its unedited form, but acknowledges that the proof was rushed to publication so that it could compete with Alpöge and Claude.

“The PDF below was posted on Nov. 20 on Ravi Vakil’s blog,” Masullo wrote on a Google site. “It was never meant to be shared publicly at this stage, and it has been posted in this draft form in response to current circumstances.”

It’s entirely possible that future revisions of Masullo’s work may solve the problems in the early draft and create a fully human proof of the Riemann Hypothesis without AI, but that isn’t happening anytime soon.

This is a lot of information about finding the Riemann Hypothesis, so it’s probably a good idea to briefly explain what it even is. In the 1730s, famous mathematician Leonhard Euler came up with a zeta function as a way to solve the Basel Problem, another mathematical curiosity about the exact sum of the reciprocals of squares. Euler was successful in this endeavor, and the zeta function became a part of mathematics.

Bernhard Riemann picked up where Euler left off and expanded the zeta function to use complex numbers — real numbers mixed with imaginary numbers — using a process called analytic continuation. Riemann used this expanded function to express how many prime numbers there were under a specific number and how tightly those prime numbers were packed together.

This is easy enough to do in your head with small numbers, like figuring out there are four prime numbers under 10, but when the biggest prime number is 41,024,320 digits long, having a function to do it for you is a lot more helpful.

The mechanics of Riemann’s expanded zeta function are quite complicated, and the math-focused YouTube channel Numberphile has an excellent explainer from a professional mathematician (with pictures) if you want to learn more.

The hypothesis concerns the solutions the function yields. Riemann’s version of the zeta function showed that if you plugged in an even negative number, like -2, -4 or -672, the function would always spit out a zero. These are referred to as trivial zeroes, and Riemann proved that this was always true in his original paper.

The Riemann Hypothesis is the conjecture that all the other numbers that would also make a zero — referred to as non-trivial zeroes — follow a very specific formula, which is “½ + it”, where “i” is an imaginary number and “t” is any real number, positive or negative. In short, Riemann believed that there was no other way to generate a zero with his zeta function other than even negative numbers (trivial zeroes) and numbers that followed the “½+it” formula (non-trivial zeroes). Riemann provided some examples of the hypothesis being right but never wrote a full proof of it.

It’s worth noting that not every number that follows the “½+it” formula produces a zero, but that all the numbers that produce a zero will use that formula. It’s kind of the same as saying that all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares.

In the 167 years since the hypothesis was first published, mathematicians have found 12 trillion non-trivial zeroes, and every single one of them fits the above rules. Trillions of other numbers that don’t follow those rules have been tested to find a counterexample, since even one counterexample disproves the hypothesis immediately. Those efforts have produced no counterexamples at all.

This isn’t conclusive proof, but it’s such an overwhelming amount of evidence that mathematicians began assuming that the hypothesis was true, even if no one could prove it. Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is the first to show in any context that the hypothesis is always true, which, according to Tetali, has implications in prime number understanding, number theory and other branches of mathematics.

“The big job on the math side is to find a human-understandable proof,” Lagarias said. “I would say this is certainly going to happen; there will be such understanding. Already there are several AI digests of the proof breaking it into its component pieces. I have seen one [that’s] 11 pages, 164 pages, 273 pages. There are great ideas to extract from them.”

But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it

A new feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

The new app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. The videos cover all the key areas of your body to give you a full workout.

Some of the new features, such as the strength videos, will be available to all iPhone users. But the ones that rely on AI will run only on phones that support Apple Intelligence. #3099. Is the AI Trade Ending?

Investors backing AI have a lot to think about.

By Motley Fool Staff – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:19PM EST

In this podcast, Motley Fool contributors Travis Hoium and Lou Whiteman and Motley Fool analyst Emily Flippen discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Nov. 6, 2026.

Travis Hoium: Is the AI trade ending? Motley Fool Hidden Gems investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gem’s investing. I'm Travis Hoium, joined today by Lou Whiteman and Emily Flippen. Guys, we've got to start with the big news for the week. We had some panic in the markets, I would say, on Thursday. The NASDAQ, I believe, was down about 5%. S&P 500 down four or 5%. Really big moves in some of the big names that have had a really great year in the AI trade. Lou, the broad question is, is this AI trade dead? Is it ending? Is it slowing down? Where does your head go after a week like this?

Lou Whiteman: I don't think it's dead by any means, and I actually don't think it's necessarily slowing down, but I think we are shifting, both and more in the perception of it on our side, but I think we are seeing a shift, and that will affect investments and the companies we're looking at. I think the land grab period might be over. For the last two years, it was a clear mandate: just go spend. The risk was under-investing. It was never over-investing. We all knew this was a lot of money, but we accepted that. The benefit of the doubt is gone. The market psychology is beginning to turn towards return of investment. I think it was happening already. I don't necessarily think it was just an election thing, but definitely, I think the election was the cherry on the top. I think, again, I think it can still work from here. I think these companies will continue to invest. But just this Pollyanna world where, don't worry, it will all work out in the end, which you can get a premium because you have certainty there. You assign a premium to that certainty. That certainty is gone, and people are asking questions, and that will affect valuation, and it might, long term, out.

Travis Hoium: Emily, the interesting thing this week was that we did have the election, which we don't, as investors want to focus too much on that, but it was such an interesting reaction because after-hours trading on Tuesday had the markets falling fairly significantly, a couple of percentage points. Then Wednesday was a phenomenal day. We knew the results of the election on Wednesday. Then Thursday was a terrible day. It seems like the market is just confused with itself what it wants to think about both the election. Then, like Lou said, I think maybe this is just bringing some reality and going, Wait a second. Nobody wants data centers in their backyard, and that was true across the board, no matter who won on Tuesday. It is such a strange back-and-forth that we've had just in the past three or four days.

Emily Flippen: My take might not age well, so you can hold me to it later. But I think the market was trying to do two things. One is price in the risk of new political pressure on things like data centers, which is likely going to be a big focus point when you look at our new congressional setup, but also pricing in the reality that is CapEx and spending for things like AI indicate continued growth. That's what's causing the volatility. You have two things that are acting against each other. I'm not trying to dismiss the pain that people experience this week, but I personally don't think we'll ever see a sustained downturn in AI spending or AI bubble, so to speak, until we start to see hyperscalers turning off their CapEx spend. So far, we don't have any indication that that is the case, and we likely won't get that indication until we get next quarter's earnings, when we start to get guidance for things like CapEx into fiscal year 2027.

Travis Hoium: I think you're right that right now we don't see a slowdown in CapEx spending, but I try to study history on these kinds of things. If you look at what happened in the.com buildout, which on the telecom side is probably the most analogous thing we have to this current AI buildout. There was growth in that CapEx through the end of 2000. At least the December quarter of 2000, but the market peaked in March of 2000. By a year later, the NASDAQ 100 was down about 50%. As the market is always forward-looking, are we running a risk where whether they want to blame it on political pressure and regulations or whether they want to say, Hey, you know what? Borrowing costs are going up, so we got to pull back. Stock prices are down. We don't have this mandate that Lou talked about to spend as much as we want in the future. If that spending starts to slow, typically the market drops before we actually hear that in earnings calls. Is that at least on your mind when you're looking, especially at these big cap companies, and then even down the value chain?

Emily Flippen: Well, I actually think that there are two separate things. one side, we have, say, the Telecom Giants, for instance, big hardware plays that are the recipients of CapEx spend from, let's say, the hyperscalers today.

Travis Hoium: Do you put Nvidia in that category, too?

Emily Flippen: I would put Nvidia in that category. That's a great example. People look towards Nvidia whenever they report earnings as the AI leader. But in practice, Nvidia is a lagging indicator of spend that has already happened. We can continue to see growth with Nvidia while the market is selling off because what they're selling off, to your point, is what the future expectations are. I personally think a lot of those future expectations and regards to growth and CapEx come from a lot of these large software players that can, to your point, turn off and turn on that dial very quickly, and then that will dovetail all the way down the chain to the big hardware players.

Travis Hoium: Lou, we got to talk a little bit about mindset on a week like this because I think this is where the Motley Fools' long-term mindset, having a multi-year, maybe even multi-decade view, really comes into play because we have no idea what's going to happen with the market tomorrow or the next or next week. But if you have a view on what's going to happen five years from now, ten years from now, that should put things in your favor a little bit. How are you handling a week like this? Is there any actions that you're taking? Are you doing nothing? Are you finding opportunities? Where are you at as an investor?

Lou Whiteman: I actually had the best place to be on Thursday when all this was going down. I was in a small metal tube without any access. I was on an airplane.

Travis Hoium: Were you testing Starling for us?

Lou Whiteman: No, I was on Delta. The Wi-Fi was fine, but I wasn't doing a lot of trading. But actually, it's perfect. I was handcuffed, even if I wanted to, but look, it's so easy to get caught up in the moment, and it is, like I said, I do think there's a shift here, and I don't want to whistle past it because I do think, to butcher the old fable, once nobody ever could picture the emperor with his clothes on again after they all realized. I think change can be permanent here, but I still think, if you look at it, AI is not going away. Whatever it's going to become, whether it's the imaginary friend on your shoulder or just a productivity machine, there is a real there there, and there are long-term trends that you can look at there. There was a lot of carnage just almost everywhere. There was risk on, including my beloved space sector. I think that I can still see. I don't know what the next six months are going to look like. I'm a little nervous about the next six months. Looking long term, there are trends that are going to work out, and I do think there will be buying opportunities. I do think, look, even going back to 1999, there were winners there. One of the lessons is that there's never been a bubble, and this is a bubble. It doesn't mean it's going to burst, but anytime there's enthusiasm about a sector, and it gets too crazy valuations, it's a bubble. May it long last, but there will always be winners and losers. I think it is probably time for us to try and look at the world in that way instead of this euphoria of everything works out.

Travis Hoium: Emily, you're in the room trying to pick stocks each month. Are you seeing more opportunities today, or are you seeing more risk?

Emily Flippen: I see a bit of both, to be honest with you, and it really depends on a company-by-company basis because I think, to lose points, AI can be an existential risk, and I know we saw a lot of that this earnings season. At the same time, there are great companies that are going, in my opinion, to come out the other side of this that the market is punishing, and I know we're going to talk about some of them later in the show. But the market just doesn't understand today how to price a lot of companies. In my opinion, that creates opportunities, but it does mean that you have to have the stomach for pretty intense levels of volatility because with great opportunity, does come great risk. In the market today, there's a lot of mispricing happening. Therefore, there's a lot of risk and a lot of confusion.

Travis Hoium: In a moment, we're going to talk about some of those potential opportunities. You're listening to Motley Fool and Jim's Investing. Welcome back to Motley Fool, Hidden Gems Investing. My big question for today is: are these non-AI stocks back? A couple that caught my eye this week- maybe it's because I owned shares, but Duolingo jumped, I think, about 35% after their reported earnings. Their daily active user growth was phenomenal. #3098. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.
